opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the interesting thing is that the way people use these models is changing. Early on, you'd ask a question and get a few paragraphs back, and if that took a few seconds, nobody really cared because you were reading at human speed anyway. But more and more, the model isn't just producing text for a person to read. It's thinking, reasoning through a problem, writing code, calling tools, checking its own work, maybe exploring several approaches in parallel and then picking the best one. In that world, most of the tokens being generated are never read by a human at all. They're intermediate computation.

So if you want a model to do a lot of reasoning before it gives you an answer, the latency of that whole chain really matters. At a hundred tokens a second, a long chain of thought that's tens of thousands of tokens takes minutes. At ten thousand tokens a second, that same amount of thinking happens in a couple of seconds. That's a qualitative change in what you can do interactively. You can afford to have the model think much harder, try many more candidate solutions, and still feel responsive.

And it compounds in agentic settings. If you have a system that's doing many steps, each step generating a lot of tokens, the per-token speed is basically your wall-clock bottleneck. Making that two orders of magnitude faster means tasks that would take an hour could take under a minute.

The reason it's a hardware question is that generation is fundamentally sequential and tends to be bound by memory bandwidth rather than raw compute. Each new token requires reading the model's weights and the attention state, and you're doing very little arithmetic per byte you move. So getting to really high tokens per second for a single stream is less about adding more FLOPs and more about rethinking memory systems, how close the weights sit to the compute, interconnect between chips, and how you partition the model. Combine that with software techniques like speculative decoding, distillation into smaller models, and quantization, and I think very high generation speeds become achievable. It's a co-design problem across models, systems, and hardware, which is exactly the kind of thing that makes it a worthwhile target.

r001.rationale: It says faster generation lets a model spend much more time thinking through a problem, including long chains of thought that would otherwise take minutes.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the model can try many more candidate solutions and explore several approaches in parallel.

r003.rationale: It mentions generating code and intermediate reasoning tokens, but does not distinguish the number of tokens spent reasoning about code from the size of the resulting code.

r004.rationale: It says the model can check its work and choose the best approach, but does not say that more reasoning tokens could make the resulting code easier to read.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the interesting thing about 10,000 tokens per second is that it's not just a quantitative change, it's a qualitative one. Today, most of our interactions with these models are sort of conversational pace. You ask a question, you watch the tokens stream out at something like reading speed, and that shapes how you think about using the model. It feels like talking to a person.

But if you can generate, say, a hundred times faster than that, the model stops being something you converse with and starts being something you can use as a component inside a larger system. You can have the model explore many possibilities in parallel, generate a bunch of candidate solutions, evaluate them, discard most of them, and keep the best ones, all in the time it currently takes to produce one answer. Search over the space of possible outputs becomes practical. Long chains of reasoning, where the model might need to produce tens of thousands of intermediate tokens before it arrives at a useful conclusion, go from being something you'd wait minutes for to something that's essentially instantaneous from the user's point of view.

And I think that's the key: a lot of what we want these systems to do, like writing and testing and revising a substantial piece of software, or reasoning through a hard scientific question, involves a lot of generated text that the user never actually needs to read. It's scaffolding. If generating that scaffolding is expensive and slow, you don't do it. If it's cheap and fast, you do a lot more of it, and the quality of the final result goes up.

From the hardware side, the reason I think it's a good target is that it forces you to confront the real bottlenecks. Decoding is fundamentally a memory-bandwidth problem. You're streaming the weights, and increasingly the KV cache, through the chip for every token, and the arithmetic intensity is low. Getting to 10,000 tokens per second for a single sequence means you have to think seriously about keeping model state in very fast memory, about how you partition a model across many chips with really low-latency interconnect, about speculative techniques, and about what the model architecture itself should look like. Those are all questions you'd be happy to ignore if you were optimizing for aggregate throughput over a big batch. Having a concrete, somewhat uncomfortable number keeps you honest about per-sequence latency, which I think is where a lot of the value actually is.

r001.rationale: It says faster generation makes long chains of reasoning involving tens of thousands of intermediate tokens practical.

r002.rationale: It says the model could explore many possibilities in parallel, generate candidate solutions, and keep the best ones.

r003.rationale: It describes generated text as scaffolding for software work, but does not distinguish reasoning-token count from the size of the resulting code.

r004.rationale: It says more scaffolding can improve final-result quality, but does not say the resulting code would be better to read.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the interesting thing about 10,000 tokens per second is that it lets you use generation in ways that aren’t really practical today. It’s much faster than a person can read, so the point isn’t to put text on the screen faster. It’s to let the system do more work before it gives you an answer.

For a difficult question, you might want it to explore several approaches, check its work, and revise a solution. If that takes thousands of tokens, generation speed determines whether you get an interactive experience or have to walk away and come back later. At 10,000 tokens per second, you can fit a lot more of that work into a second or two.

So I view it as a useful target for hardware design: can we make that kind of computation fast enough, and efficient enough, that it becomes something you can use routinely? Speed doesn’t guarantee a better answer, but it gives you room to do substantially more computation within the same response time.

r001.rationale: It says the model can use thousands of tokens to explore approaches, check its work, and revise before answering, conveying more tokens spent on reasoning.

r002.rationale: It mentions exploring several approaches but does not identify parallel rollouts as an opportunity.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss generated code or distinguish reasoning-token count from resulting code size.

r004.rationale: It does not connect reasoning about generated code to the readability of the resulting code.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the interesting thing about 10,000 tokens per second is that it changes what you can do within a reasonable latency budget. If you need a response in a second, you could generate a fairly short answer, or you could have the system explore several approaches, check its work, and then give you an answer. Much faster generation gives you room to do that extra computation without making the user wait.

And for specialized hardware, that’s an interesting target because generating tokens sequentially puts very different demands on the system than training does. You want to design the computation, memory, and communication together around that workload. The exact number isn’t magical, but that level of speed could enable much richer reasoning and much more responsive interactions.

r001.rationale: The response says faster generation gives the system room for extra computation, including exploring approaches and checking its work, and describes enabling richer reasoning.

r002.rationale: It mentions exploring several approaches but does not identify parallel rollouts.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish tokens spent reasoning about generated code from the size of the resulting code.

r004.rationale: It says nothing about reasoning improving the readability of generated code.
